titre: William Smith, 1815: Fossils, Not Rock, Make the Map
accroche: In 1815, William Smith publishes a map on which the strata of England and Wales are recognized by their fossils. In 1819, he is in prison.
contenu_vulgarise:
Once assembled, William Smith's map measures 259 by 176 centimeters. It consists of fifteen sheets at a scale of five miles to the inch, printed on a base map ordered from John Cary: county boundaries and much of the relief were removed to let the strata show. The Geological Society of London states that it was not actually put on sale until September 1815, even though every copy bears the date August 1815.

## The idea: a stratum is recognized by its fossils

Smith notices that rock strata can be recognized by the fossils they contain, and that they always follow one another in the same order. He can therefore predict where to find a given type of rock across the country, without depending on the look of the rock alone. To do so he assembles a fossil collection that serves as his evidence for ordering the strata: the Natural History Museum in London holds more than 2,000 of them today.

The road is long. His first geological map, that of Bath, dates from 1799. In 1801, he plots seven strata on an existing map of England and Wales. It then takes fourteen years to gather enough information and funding. Publication is by subscription, with about 400 copies issued, of which fewer than 10% are known today. Unmounted sheets cost 5 pounds 5 shillings, the varnished version on spring rollers 12 pounds.

## First map of a country?

This map is often presented as the first geological map of an entire nation. The claim needs a qualification: William Maclure's map of the United States had preceded it by six years. What Smith is the first to do is cover such an expanse, more than 175,000 square kilometers, with 23 colored strata and such detail.

## The story of the ruin

The rest of his story is known in serial form: Smith, ruined, thrown into prison, because George Bellas Greenough, president of the Geological Society, supposedly copied his map. The dates don't fit. Smith is arrested twice for debt in 1814, then spends ten weeks in King's Bench debtors' prison in 1819. Greenough's map bears the date 1819 but appears in May 1820, after that imprisonment. His debts come from a mortgage on his Tucking Mill estate and a Bath stone quarry that went badly. To pay them off in part, he sells his collection to the British Museum for 700 pounds.

Recognition comes late. In 1831, the Geological Society awards him the first Wollaston Medal, and its president, Adam Sedgwick, names him the father of English geology: sixteen years after the map.

repere.texte: The 1815 map: fifteen sheets, 259 × 176 cm assembled, five miles to the inch, about 400 copies issued, of which fewer than 10% are known today.
repere.source: Natural History Museum, London, “Britain's first geological map”; Geological Society of London, online exhibition on William Smith

carte.punch: In 1815, Smith mapped the strata by their fossils, not by how the rock looks.
carte.idee: In 1815, William Smith publishes a fifteen-sheet map on which each stratum is identified by its fossils and traced across the country. It took him fourteen years to fund it, and the debtors' prison of 1819 did not come from plagiarism.

quiz.question: What does Smith rely on to recognize a stratum and follow it from one region to another?
choix: Its color, which is the same across the whole country for a given period
The fossils it contains, since the strata always follow one another in the same order
The depth at which it is found, always identical from one region to another
The name given to it by the quarrymen of each county
quiz.explication: Smith identifies each stratum by its fossils and finds that the order of succession does not vary. Color and thickness change from one region to another, and the quarrymen's local names make it impossible to compare separate counties.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Why does the story that George Bellas Greenough ruined Smith by copying his map not hold up against the dates?
choix: Because Greenough never published a geological map of England
Because Smith had already paid off all his debts before Greenough's map appeared
Because Greenough's map, dated 1819, did not appear until May 1820, after Smith's imprisonment
Because Greenough publicly admitted to copying Smith, as early as 1815
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Greenough's map bears the date 1819 but does not appear until May 1820, after the ten weeks Smith spends in debtors' prison that same year: the chronology rules out this plagiarism as the cause of his ruin.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Where do the debts that send Smith to prison in 1819 come from?
choix: From buying his collection of more than 2,000 fossils back from the British Museum
From a mortgage on Tucking Mill and a badly managed Bath quarry
From the cost of printing the fifteen sheets of the 1815 map
From a lawsuit lost against the Geological Society of London
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The text places the origin of Smith's debts in the mortgage on his Tucking Mill estate and a Bath stone quarry that went badly, which he partly clears by selling his fossil collection to the British Museum.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What qualification must be made to the idea that the 1815 map is the very first geological map of an entire nation?
choix: It was published in 1799, the year of Smith's first map, that of Bath
It was never put on sale, unlike Greenough's
It covers only a single English county
That of the United States by William Maclure preceded it by six years
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The text specifies that William Maclure's map of the United States precedes Smith's by six years; what Smith is the first to do is cover such an expanse with such detail.

quiz_supplementaire.question: How long after the publication of the map does Smith receive the first Wollaston Medal?
choix: Sixteen years, in 1831
Three years, in 1818
Six years, in 1821
Twenty-five years, in 1840
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The text specifies that in 1831, the Geological Society awards him the first Wollaston Medal, sixteen years after the 1815 map, and that its president Adam Sedgwick then names him the father of English geology.
